evidence.label: Nonsingular systems of equations over arbitrary groups

headline: Claims every nonsingular system of equations over any group is solvable in a larger group, settling Howie's conjecture.
scope: Finite systems of equations with coefficients in an arbitrary group. Lean covers the one-relator unimodular injectivity theorem behind Kervaire's conjecture, not the multi-equation theorem.
plain: An equation over a group mixes known group elements with unknowns. It is solvable if a larger group contains the original one and values for the unknowns. The first paper claims this always works when a simple count of the unknowns, done with ordinary integers, gives independent rows. A companion paper proves the one-equation case behind Kervaire's conjecture, with a Lean formalization listed.
doesNot: This does not give a Lean proof of the many-equation theorem, or say the larger group is finite or specially structured.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Murray Gerstenhaber and Oscar Rothaus, who solved nonsingular systems over finite groups and compact Lie groups
scorecard.significanceWhy: Kervaire's conjecture and Howie's conjecture are long-standing open problems in combinatorial group theory.

explanation:
Take a group A with an element a ≠ 1. Add a new unknown t and impose the equation t a t⁻¹ = 1. Conjugating back gives a = 1. So this equation destroys a, and no larger group can solve it while keeping a. Count how often t appears, with signs: +1 − 1 = 0. That count is the exponent sum. Now try t a t a² t⁻¹ = 1. Its exponent sum is 1 + 1 − 1 = 1. The Kervaire–Laudenbach question asks whether a nonzero exponent sum always prevents such collapse.

An equation over a group G is a word mixing elements of G with unknowns[1]. A solution is a larger group containing a copy of G, with values for the unknowns that make every word equal 1[1]. For several equations, the exponent sums form an integer matrix. For example, x₁x₂g and x₁x₂⁻¹h give rows (1, 1) and (1, −1). The determinant is 1·(−1) − 1·1 = −2, which is not zero. So the rows are independent. A system is nonsingular when its rows have full rank over the rationals[2].

Gerstenhaber and Rothaus in 1962 solved nonsingular systems over finite groups and compact Lie groups[3]. Howie solved them over locally indicable groups[4]. Klyachko treated one equation over torsion-free groups with exponent sum ±1[5]. The obstacle was arbitrary coefficient groups. These may have torsion, be uncountable, or have no nice finite models.

The companion paper proves the one-variable case: for every group A and every word with exponent sum ±1, A embeds in the quotient[6]. The Kervaire conjecture follows: one new generator and one new relation never kill a nontrivial group[7]. For other exponent sums d, the quotient maps onto the nontrivial cyclic group of order |d|, or onto the integers when d = 0[8].

The first paper claims the general statement. If the exponent-sum matrix has full row rank, G embeds in the quotient, so the system has a solution in an overgroup[9]. This is Howie's conjecture[10]. The proof turns a hypothetical lost element into a flat surface with disks and bands. Full row rank forces matching numbers of positive and negative disks for each equation[11]. A spectral phase function, measured through the regular representation of G, then forces the lost element to be the identity.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the one-relator theorem with exponent sum ±1. The many-equation theorem has no Lean formalization. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Lean covers the unimodular one-relator theorem behind Kervaire's conjecture, not the many-equation theorem. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A word mixing fixed group elements with unknowns, to be set equal to the identity.
A larger group that contains a copy of the original group.
The total number of times an unknown appears, counting its inverse as minus one.
A system whose matrix of exponent sums has independent rows over the rational numbers.
The smallest normal subgroup containing given elements; quotienting by it imposes those elements as relations.
Elements other than the identity that have finite order.
Every nontrivial finitely generated subgroup maps onto the integers.
